tracks.title: Interview in two weeks
tracks.audience: You have an interview soon and want the highest-yield route.
tracks.summary: Learn the method first, then the most-asked designs, then drill. The time shown counts reading only; add practice sessions.

steps.why: Learn the 45-minute script and the scoring rubric before you read any design. You will return to it at the end for three timed mock sessions.
Estimation is step 2 of every answer. Learn the latency numbers and the method.
A warm-up with caching, key generation and the 301 versus 302 trade-off.
Unique ID generation: the Snowflake layout, ticket servers, UUIDv7 and what happens when a clock moves backwards. Key generation comes up inside many designs.
Rate limiting, and the fail-open versus fail-closed choice (Stripe fails open; Envoy lets you choose).
Replication, quorums and consistent hashing, which recur everywhere.
Caching in depth: stale sets, stampedes and what happens when a cache server dies.
Real-time messaging, delivery guarantees and fan-out.
Fan-out on write versus read, the classic feed question.
Queues, priorities, retries and deduplication.
The message log in depth: partitions, replication, consumer groups and leader failover (Kafka), the engine under many queue answers.
Upload, transcoding and delivery of video.
Geospatial indexing and matching.
Idempotency and correctness with money.
Contention and double-booking.
Sagas and the outbox: the standard answer to cross-service consistency.
SLOs, error budgets and how to stop a cascading failure.
Estimation drills with worked solutions, so the arithmetic is automatic.
Practise spotting flaws in plausible designs. Some scenarios draw on incidents (C01 to C03) and AI notes outside this track; skip those or read them first.
Flashcards for the AI, streaming and observability systems (22 to 31), the primers and the incident casebook. They add facts beyond the systems above rather than repeating them.
Open scenarios that practise stating a decision and its trade-offs. Finish by running three timed mock sessions from the first step.

tracks.title: Building blocks first
tracks.audience: You are earlier in your career, or want solid foundations before full designs.
tracks.summary: The small pieces that appear inside every large design: IDs, caches, locks, counters, storage engines, load balancers and APIs.

steps.why: Start with how to estimate, so every later design has numbers.
The simplest building block: unique IDs, and what happens when clocks go wrong.
Your first complete design, built from IDs and caches.
Counters, windows and failure modes in a small system.
How data is partitioned and replicated across machines.
B-trees, LSM trees and how to choose a database.
Caching at large scale.
Leader election, locks and fencing.
Top-K, approximate counting and leaderboards.
How traffic is spread across servers.
Pagination, idempotency and evolving APIs.
Consistency across services.
CAP and PACELC without the pick-two shortcut, why R + W > N is not linearizable, and how caches fail.

tracks.title: Senior engineer to architect
tracks.audience: You design well already and want the decision-making, risk and communication side.
tracks.summary: Records of decisions, how to review, deployment shape, real failures, migrations, disaster recovery, multi-tenancy, security, reliability and cost, then exercises that ask for a justified decision.

steps.why: How architects decide, record and defend decisions: ADRs, design docs and boring technology.
How to review a change or a design: reading order, comment labels, and a separate routine for AI-generated code.
A deployment process that bypassed staging: read the incident, then write your own safeguards.
Automated failover meeting split writes: availability versus integrity.
Reliability as a design input: SLOs, error budgets and postmortems.
Replacing parts of a running system safely.
Monolith or microservices: the premium Fowler describes, Shopify's modular monolith, Prime Video's consolidation of one service, and Conway's law.
Threat modeling and zero trust at design time.
What drives cost and how to talk about it.
Multi-tenancy: isolation is not authentication, silo versus pool, and the noisy-neighbour mitigations. Cost and limits per tenant follow from the cost primer.
Privacy as architecture: minimisation, purpose limitation enforced in infrastructure, and deletion that reaches every copy.
A control plane and data plane at scale, with steering.
A design where correctness dominates everything else.
Event sourcing and CQRS: when a history of changes is worth the cost, what it does to consistency, and the lighter alternatives. Compare with how payments get correctness from idempotency.
The shared coordination service many systems depend on, and its risks.
A routine operation with too much blast radius.
Recovery tools that depend on the thing that failed.
RTO, RPO and the four disaster-recovery strategies, and why recovery that depends on the failing system, or is never rehearsed, does not work.
Deployment verification, dead code and kill switches.
Hidden resource limits and dependency cascades.
Eight open scenarios: write the decision record, then compare with what a strong answer covers.
Review flawed designs the way a design review would.
Review a flawed API spec, then check yourself against the key: authorisation first, compatibility last.

tracks.title: AI platform engineer
tracks.audience: You run the models or the infrastructure around them yourself: serving, retrieval indexes, fine-tuning or training.
tracks.summary: LLM basics, then serving, vector search and retrieval, agents, evaluation, improving models and learning from feedback, followed by security and cost. If you only call hosted model APIs, take the AI application architect track.

steps.why: Start here, section 1 only (about 10 minutes): after it you can explain tokens, the context window, why a model keeps no memory between calls and why its outputs vary. The rest of P19 is optional on this track.
After this you can size a KV cache, explain why time to first token and time per output token are separate targets, and say what continuous batching and splitting prefill from decode buy.
After this you can choose between an in-memory graph index, an SSD-resident index and pgvector for a corpus size and recall target, and say what each costs in memory.
After this you can design a retrieval pipeline end to end (chunking, hybrid search, reranking, permission filtering) and explain why most wrong answers are retrieval failures.
After this you can design the platform under an agent: tool calls, MCP, sandboxes, saved state and step, time and cost budgets.
After this you can decide whether a second agent is worth it, pick a topology and say how you would compare it with one agent at equal cost.
After this you can design an evaluation: graders, regression and capability suites, several trials, and when to report pass@k or pass^k.
After this you can choose between prompting, adapters and full fine-tuning, explain RLHF with PPO and DPO in an interview, and gate a rollout on evals.
After this you can design a two-stage recommender and explain the feedback loops that learning from user behaviour creates.
After this you can tell a bandit problem from full RL, design a reward and its logging, and explain how RL trains reasoning models. Read sections 1 to 3 and 8 first.
Optional, if you train models: after this you can explain data, tensor and pipeline parallelism, checkpointing, and why failures dominate at thousands of GPUs.
After this you can defend an LLM system against prompt injection with the Rule of Two, and keep long agent runs alive with checkpoints, limits and tracing.
After this you can run a threat model on any design in this track: trust boundaries, STRIDE and a response to each threat.
After this you can estimate the dominant cost (GPU hours or tokens) and name each lever with what it gives up.
Practise: exercises 6, 7 and 8 ask for an AI design decision. Write the decision record, then compare with the answer key.
Finish with a 45-minute mock interview on note 23 or 25 using this script and rubric. It brings serving, retrieval, agents, evaluation, security and cost together.

tracks.title: AI application architect
tracks.audience: You build products by calling hosted model APIs and want to know which pattern fits, and how it fails in production.
tracks.summary: From one model call to workflows, agents and multi-agent systems, then production engineering, evaluation, security and cost. If you run the models yourself, take the AI platform engineer track.

steps.why: Start here: after it you can explain tokens, context and sampling, and choose between one model call, a workflow and an agent for a feature.

After this you can design retrieval for a product (chunking, hybrid search, reranking, permission filtering), the most common way to give a model your data. Note 24 explains the indexes if you want depth.
After this you can design what sits under a single agent: tool calls, MCP, sandboxes, saved state and budgets.
After this you can decide whether a second agent is worth it, pick a topology and say how you would compare it with one agent at equal cost.
Reference, skim: what MCP, A2A and the main frameworks are and what changed in 2026. Come back to it when you pick a stack.
After this you can defend an LLM product against prompt injection with the Rule of Two, and keep long agent runs alive with checkpoints, limits, caching and tracing.
After this you can design an evaluation: graders, regression and capability suites, several trials, and when to report pass@k or pass^k.
Optional: after it you can tell when a product should learn from outcomes (bandits, RL-trained models, game agents) and design a reward that is hard to game. Read sections 1 to 3 and 8 first.
After this you can threat-model the trust boundaries an agent adds: tool results, credentials and external actions.
After this you can put a number on cost per task in tokens and choose model tiers and budgets.
Practise: exercises 6, 7 and 8 (an account assistant, workflow or agent, one agent or several). Write the decision record, then compare with the answer key.
Finish with a 45-minute mock interview on note 23 or 25 using this script and rubric.

tracks.title: The whole atlas in learning order
tracks.audience: You want to study systematically over several weeks.
tracks.summary: All 42 systems, from foundations to AI, in the order the stages build on each other.
